content: Syphilis is a bacterial sexually transmitted infection caused by Treponema pallidum. It is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. The prevalence is highest in the WHO African Region, with approximately 5% of males aged 15–49 years affected. Mother-to-child transmission of syphilis, known as congenital syphilis, can occur if the infection in the pregnant woman is not detected and treated early. Congenital syphilis often leads to devastating outcomes for the fetus, including stillbirth, neonatal death, preterm birth, or low birth weight. In 2012, an estimated 350,000 adverse pregnancy outcomes were attributed to syphilis globally, including 143,000 early fetal deaths or stillbirths, 62,000 neonatal deaths, 44,000 preterm or low-birth-weight infants, and 102,000 infected infants. Untreated syphilis during pregnancy, particularly primary and secondary stages, typically results in severe adverse outcomes, including fetal death in a substantial proportion of cases. Even latent syphilis infections during pregnancy can lead to serious complications in more than half of cases. The burden of congenital syphilis is highest in lowand middle-income countries, particularly in the WHO African Region. However, congenital syphilis is preventable through effective early screening and treatment strategies during pregnancy. If the mother receives adequate treatment early in pregnancy, ideally before the second trimester, the fetus can be cured, and the risk of adverse outcomes is minimal. Global efforts to screen and treat pregnant women for syphilis have begun to reduce mother-to-child transmission rates. Syphilis is transmitted through sexual contact with infectious lesions on mucous membranes or abraded skin, via blood transfusion, or transplacentally from a pregnant woman to her fetus. If untreated, the disease progresses through stages over many years. Early syphilis includes primary, secondary, and early latent stages, while late syphilis includes late latent and tertiary stages. Primary syphilis typically presents as a solitary, painless chancre at the site of inoculation, such as the vagina, penis, or anus, after an incubation period of approximately 21 days. The lesion begins as a raised papule, ulcerates, and heals within 3 to 10 weeks, with or without treatment. Secondary syphilis occurs 4 to 8 weeks after the primary lesion and is characterized by generalized mucocutaneous lesions, often involving the palms and soles. These lesions may be accompanied by systemic symptoms such as malaise, fever, and lymphadenopathy. Secondary syphilis resolves spontaneously, even without treatment, and progresses to the latent stage if untreated. Latent syphilis is defined by positive serology without clinical symptoms or signs. It is categorized into early latent (infection for less than two years) and late latent (infection for two years or more). Sexual transmission typically occurs during the primary, secondary, and early latent stages, while mother-to-child transmission can occur up to several years after initial infection. If untreated, most patients remain in the latent stage, but approximately 25% develop tertiary syphilis, which can affect any organ system decades after infection. Tertiary syphilis manifests as neurosyphilis, cardiovascular syphilis, or gummatous lesions. Neurosyphilis can occur at any stage and may present with acute mental status changes, meningitis, stroke, cranial nerve dysfunction, or ocular abnormalities. Late neurosyphilis, occurring 10–30 years after infection, is characterized by tabes dorsalis and general paresis. Congenital syphilis most commonly results in secondor third-trimester fetal loss or premature labor. Serologic testing for syphilis should be performed for all mothers with stillborn infants to document evidence of infection. Infants born to seropositive mothers should be examined for signs of congenital syphilis, including bullous rash, rhinitis, laryngitis, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, osteochondritis, periostitis, meningitis, and chorioretinitis. Late congenital syphilis in children over two years of age may present with inflammatory manifestations affecting the eyes, ears, joints, or skeletal malformations. The WHO defines congenital syphilis as a stillbirth, live birth, or fetal loss in a seropositive mother without adequate treatment, or a live birth or child under two years of age with clinical or microbiological evidence of syphilis infection. Direct detection methods for syphilis include dark-field microscopy, direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing, and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). Dark-field microscopy is highly specific but requires specialized equipment and expertise, with sensitivity below 50%. DFA testing uses fluorescence microscopy to detect spirochetes stained with fluorescein-labeled antibodies, offering higher sensitivity and specificity than dark-field microscopy. NAATs detect T. pallidum DNA using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and are highly sensitive but not widely available commercially. Serologic testing for syphilis includes non-treponemal and treponemal tests. Non-treponemal tests, such as the Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) and Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR) tests, detect anti-lipid antibodies but may yield false-positive results in other conditions. Treponemal tests, including the Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay (TPHA) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorbed (FTA-ABS) test, are highly specific but do not differentiate between active and treated infections. A confirmed diagnosis requires positive results from both test types. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for treponemal antibodies provide results within 10–15 minutes and are suitable for use in resource-limited settings.
